title: Build a tiny hash map
summary: Put, get, remove and grow: the inside of Dictionary<TKey, TValue>, written by hand.

steps.title: Buckets of key/value pairs
body: A hash map is an array of buckets, and each bucket is a short list of `(Key, Value)` pairs.
**Put** goes to the key's bucket and looks through it: if the key is already there, overwrite its value; otherwise append a new pair.

To keep the trace predictable it uses a toy hash, the key's **length**. `"ant"` and `"bee"` both have length 3 and collide in bucket 0. Watch the second `Put("ant", ...)` **replace** the value instead of adding a duplicate.

code: var buckets = new List<(string Key, int Value)>[3];
for (var b = 0; b < buckets.Length; b++) buckets[b] = new();

steps.explain: `cat`, `yak` and `emu` have length 3, so they share bucket 0. The second `ox` overwrites the first, so bucket 2 holds one pair.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines of `TryGet`, which finds a key's value or reports that it is missing.
lines: bool TryGet(string key, out int value)
if (pair.Key == key) { value = pair.Value; return true; }

steps.explain: Only the key's own bucket is searched: that is the whole trick. `value = 0` is required because an `out` parameter must be set on every path.

steps.title: Search a bucket
prompt: Write `int FindIndex(List<(string Key, int Value)> bucket, string key)`: the position of the pair whose `Key` equals `key`, or `-1`.
You will reuse this idea in `Put`, `TryGet` and `Remove`.
starter: int FindIndex(List<(string Key, int Value)> bucket, string key)
solution: int FindIndex(List<(string Key, int Value)> bucket, string key)
template: var dojoB = new List<(string Key, int Value)> { ("ant", 1), ("bee", 2), ("cow", 3) };
Dojo.Eq("an empty bucket gives -1", -1, FindIndex(new List<(string Key, int Value)>(), "ant"));
hints: Loop with an index: `if (bucket[i].Key == key) return i;`

steps.title: Growing means rehashing
body: When the load factor gets too high, the map allocates **twice as many buckets**. But a key's bucket is `hash % bucketCount`, so changing the count changes where keys belong.
Every pair must be **rehashed**: re-inserted into the new array using the new count.
In .NET, `key.GetHashCode()` gives the hash. Use `(hash & int.MaxValue) % buckets.Length` to clear the sign bit so the bucket is never negative.

steps.prompt: A map grows from 4 buckets to 8. Integer key `6` was in bucket `6 % 4 = 2`. Where is it after rehashing?
steps.explain: `6 % 8` is 6. Leaving it in bucket 2 would make it unfindable, because lookups now compute `6 % 8`.

code: buckets = new List<(string Key, int Value)>[__1__];
for (var b = 0; b < buckets.Length; b++) buckets[b] = new();
steps.explain: `BucketOf` uses the **new** `buckets.Length`, so every key moves to the right place for the bigger table.

steps.title: TinyMap
prompt: Write a class `TinyMap` from `string` keys to `int` values, without `Dictionary` or `HashSet`:
- `int Count` and `int BucketCount` (properties). It starts with **4** buckets.
- `void Put(string key, int value)`: add, or overwrite an existing key.
- `bool Remove(string key)`: `true` if the key was there.
- After a `Put` that adds a key, if `Count > BucketCount * 3 / 4`, double the buckets and rehash.
Use `(key.GetHashCode() & int.MaxValue) % buckets.Length` as the bucket.

forbid.message: Does not use Dictionary or HashSet

hints: Write a private `FindIndex` helper and use it in `Put`, `TryGet` and `Remove`.
In `Put`, only a **new** key increments `Count` and can trigger `Grow()`.
`Grow`: keep the old array, make one twice as big, and add every pair to `buckets[BucketOf(pair.Key)]`.
